items.stem: When Siddhartha enters the chamber, where does he stand?
items.quote: Siddhartha entered the chamber, where his father was sitting on a mat of bast, and stepped behind his father and remained standing there, until his father felt that someone was standing behind him.
items.why: He waits quietly to be noticed before he speaks his request.

items.stem: When the father looks in after the moon has risen, what is on Siddhartha's legs?
items.quote: Through the window of the chamber he looked back inside; there stood Siddhartha, not moving from his spot, his arms folded, moonlight reflecting from his bare shins.
items.why: The moonlit detail shows how long Siddhartha has stood there.

items.stem: At dawn, what part of Siddhartha does the father touch?
items.quote: The Father touched Siddhartha’s shoulder.
items.why: A single touch marks the moment the father lets his son go.

items.stem: In the night, how does Siddhartha's robe look to his watching father?
items.quote: Pale shimmered his bright robe.
items.why: Even in the dark, the father can see that his son has not moved.

items.stem: After their first talk, the father goes to bed indignant.
items.quote: Indignant, the father left the chamber; indignant, he went to his bed and lay down.
items.why: The father's anger is the first obstacle to Siddhartha's plan.

items.stem: Siddhartha tells Govinda he will begin the Samana life in a week.
items.quote: Tomorrow, at daybreak I will begin the life of the Samanas.
items.why: He means to leave at once: tomorrow at daybreak.

items.stem: Complete Siddhartha's reply: “I will stand and ____.”
items.quote: “I will stand and wait.”
items.why: His patient answer turns waiting into a quiet act of will.

items.stem: Complete Siddhartha's words: “My desire is to become a ____.”
items.quote: My desire is to become a Samana.
items.why: He names his goal plainly before his father.

items.stem: Match each person to what they do in the chapter.
items.why: Each person's action shows their place in Siddhartha's story.
evidence: Slowly, the Brahmin rose; Siddhartha stood silently, his arms folded.
May my father not oppose this.”
He loved Siddhartha’s eye and sweet voice

items.stem: Put these events in story order.
items.why: The night moves from request, to anger, to a gentle release.

cards.text: The father goes to bed indignant

evidence: Siddhartha entered the chamber
he went to his bed and lay down
The Father touched Siddhartha’s shoulder.

items.stem: In ¶5, who is the “he” who loved Siddhartha's eye and sweet voice?
items.quote: He loved Siddhartha’s eye and sweet voice, he loved his walk
items.why: Govinda's devotion explains why he will follow Siddhartha later.

items.stem: Near dawn, the father asks whether Siddhartha will abandon what?
items.quote: “So will you abandon your plan?”
items.why: The father is still hoping his son will give up.

items.stem: Which warning does the father give Siddhartha during the night?
items.quote: “You will fall asleep, Siddhartha.”
items.why: The father tries to wear down his son's resolve with plain facts.

items.stem: Under the banyan tree, what is Siddhartha ready to speak as he sits down?
items.quote: While putting himself down, ready to speak the Om, Siddhartha repeated murmuring the verse:
items.why: The sacred syllable Om is the focus of his meditation.

items.stem: The father takes his hand from his son's shoulder and goes outside.
items.quote: He took his hand from the shoulder of his son and went outside.
items.why: The father's quiet exit ends the standoff.

items.stem: After he rises, the father orders Siddhartha to leave the house at once.
items.quote: “What are you waiting for?”
items.why: He asks a question instead of giving an order; the standoff begins.

items.stem: Complete the father's question: “Is that you, ____?”
items.quote: Quoth the Brahmin: “Is that you, Siddhartha?
items.why: The father knows who stands behind him; the formal exchange shows the respect between them.

items.stem: Match each word to the moment it belongs to.
items.why: Each detail marks a stage of Siddhartha's leaving.
evidence: Through the small window of the chamber he looked back inside, and there he saw Siddhartha standing, his arms folded, not moving from his spot.
While putting himself down, ready to speak the Om, Siddhartha repeated murmuring the verse:
Indignant, the father left the chamber; indignant, he went to his bed and lay down.

items.stem: Put these events from the first talk in order.
items.why: The father's restless night is told step by step.

cards.text: The father asks what he awaits

Slowly, the Brahmin rose

items.stem: Put these moments of the long night in order.
items.why: The watch stretches through the night as question meets answer.

cards.text: He asks again what he awaits

evidence: Through the window of the chamber he looked back inside; there stood Siddhartha, not moving from his spot, his arms folded, moonlight reflecting from his bare shins.
he spoke, “what are you waiting for?”
“Will you always stand that way and wait, until it becomes morning, noon, and evening?”
“I will stand and wait.”

items.stem: Why does the father get up after an hour and leave the house?
items.quote: After an hour, since no sleep had come over his eyes, the Brahmin stood up, paced to and fro, and left the house.
items.why: His sleeplessness shows that the conflict troubles him more than his anger admits.

items.stem: After seeing his son still standing in the moonlight, what feeling does the father carry back to bed?
items.quote: With worry in his heart, the father went back to bed.
items.why: Worry replacing anger marks the father's first softening.

items.stem: What does Siddhartha feel all his learning has failed to do for him?
items.quote: never had he reached it completely, never had he quenched the ultimate thirst
items.why: This unmet thirst is the motive that sends him to the Samanas.

items.stem: Why does the father tell Siddhartha “You will fall asleep”?
items.quote: “You will fall asleep, Siddhartha.”
items.why: The father tries reason and consequence instead of force.

items.stem: By answering “I will stand and wait,” Siddhartha shows he will not leave without his father's consent.
items.quote: “I will stand and wait.”
items.why: He chooses patience over defiance, and that choice wins the night.

items.stem: Siddhartha doubts the holy verses because they say nothing about one's innermost part.
items.quote: was written there, and it was written that man in his sleep, in his deep sleep, would meet with his innermost part and would reside in the Atman.
items.why: The verses do speak of it; his doubt is that knowing the words is not reaching it.

items.stem: Siddhartha wonders where Atman is found: “where else but in one's own ____”
items.quote: where else but in one’s own self
items.why: If Atman lives within, then rituals and teachers cannot hand it to him.

items.stem: Govinda did not want to be one of the “tens of thousands of ____.”
items.quote: not one of those tens of thousands of Brahmins
items.why: Govinda's wish for something higher explains why he follows his friend.

items.stem: Match each cause to its effect.
items.why: The chapter links small causes to the father's changing heart.
evidence: After an hour, since no sleep had come over his eyes, the Brahmin stood up, paced to and fro, and left the house.
With worry in his heart, the father went back to bed.
May my father not oppose this.

items.stem: Order the father's changing responses.
items.why: The father moves from anger to worry to blessing.
evidence: Indignant, the father left the chamber; indignant, he went to his bed and lay down.
With worry in his heart, the father went back to bed.
The Father touched Siddhartha’s shoulder.
He took his hand from the shoulder of his son and went outside.

items.stem: Which phrase best shows Siddhartha still honors his father while doubting the Brahmins' path?
items.quote: Siddhartha knew many venerable Brahmins, chiefly his father, the pure one, the scholar, the most venerable one.
items.why: His doubt is not contempt: he leaves a father he reveres.

items.stem: In ¶5, Govinda's love is told as “he loved … he loved … he loved.” What does the repetition convey?
items.quote: He loved Siddhartha’s eye and sweet voice, he loved his walk
items.why: The piled-up 'he loved' shows a devotion strong enough to follow Siddhartha anywhere.

items.stem: “Who else was to be worshipped but Him, the only one, the Atman?” suggests worship belongs to whom?
items.quote: For whom else were offerings to be made, who else was to be worshipped but Him, the only one, the Atman?
items.why: His question quietly challenges the many offerings to many gods.

items.stem: The repeated image of Siddhartha's folded arms (¶25, ¶29, ¶30) chiefly suggests what?
items.quote: Slowly, the Brahmin rose; Siddhartha stood silently, his arms folded.
items.why: A fixed posture shows a fixed decision.

items.stem: “Will you always stand that way and wait, until it becomes morning, noon, and evening?” What does the list of times stress?
items.quote: “Will you always stand that way and wait, until it becomes morning, noon, and evening?”
items.why: Stretching the wait across a whole day shows the father measuring his son's stubbornness.

items.stem: In the dark, “Pale shimmered his bright robe” makes the still, silent Siddhartha seem almost ghostly to his watching father.
items.quote: Pale shimmered his bright robe.
items.why: The eerie image prepares the father's sense that his son is already slipping away from him.

items.stem: When Govinda speaks to him, Siddhartha answers at once, fully alert and eager to argue.
items.quote: Siddhartha looked over as if he was just waking up.
items.why: He is absorbed in his decision; he will not debate it.

items.stem: Complete the ironic line: “They knew ____, the Brahmins and their holy books”
items.quote: They knew everything, the Brahmins and their holy books, they knew everything
items.why: Knowing 'everything' yet not the way to the self is the chapter's central irony.

items.stem: Match each phrase to what it reveals.
items.why: Small phrases carry large meanings about character.
evidence: Siddhartha did not answer.
“And would you rather die, than obey your father?”
Quoth the Brahmin: “Is that you, Siddhartha?

items.stem: Order the questions in Siddhartha's reasoning in ¶8.
items.why: His questions move from the gods, to Atman, to where Atman lives.
evidence: And what about the gods?
Was it not the Atman, He, the only one, the singular one?
For whom else were offerings to be made, who else was to be worshipped but Him, the only one, the Atman?
